title: Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus/Lichen Planus Overlap Syndrome With Vitiligo-Like Depigmentation: A Case Report.
abstract: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus/lichen planus (CLE/LP) overlap syndrome is an uncommon interface dermatosis with features of both disorders. We describe a 60-year-old woman who initially developed pruritic, erythematous, scaly lesions on the dorsal hands, and facial erythema. The initial eruption resolved spontaneously within two months, without treatment, followed by persistent depigmented and erythematous patches at the previously affected sites. Wood's lamp examination accentuated the depigmentation. Histopathology of a depigmented dorsal-hand patch showed interface dermatitis with basal vacuolar alteration and a bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate. Melan-A staining on the same specimen demonstrated melanocyte loss. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showed immunoglobulin deposition at the dermoepidermal junction and shaggy fibrinogen staining. The findings supported CLE/LP overlap syndrome with subsequent vitiligo-like depigmentation. Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and once-daily topical ruxolitinib were initiated; mild repigmentation at the oral commissure was documented clinically and with Wood's lamp examination at one month. Distinguishing coexisting vitiligo from post-inflammatory melanocyte loss remains challenging, and the temporal association does not establish causality.
authors: Hasan Kh A H A Ashkanani

title: Successful Anifrolumab Treatment for Refractory Skin Lesions in Monogenic Lupus Due to C1R Deficiency.
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease exhibiting clinical heterogeneity among affected individuals. In monogenic lupus, which results from single-gene mutations, there is an early onset, atypical and severe course, and usually a familial predisposition. One of the common causes of monogenic SLE is deficiencies in the early components of the classical pathway of the complement system. We present here a 9-year-old male with hereditary C1R deficiency, suffering from chronic discoid rash since the age of 18 months, who did not sufficiently respond to conventional treatment, including topical and systemic steroids, hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, intravenous immunoglobulin, and baricitinib. Subsequently, the skin findings improved after the initiation of anifrolumab, an anti-IFNAR antibody. To the best of our knowledge, this report represents the first successful treatment of monogenic lupus and C1R deficiency with anifrolumab in the literature.
journal: Clinical medicine insights. Arthritis and musculoskeletal disorders

title: Spinal toxoplasmosis presents as myelitis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and immunosuppression: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Toxoplasmosis is a worldwide opportunistic infection that can be primary or latent, with reactivation in immunocompromised hosts. Spinal cord involvement is rare, reported almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised patients mainly those with HIV/AIDS. We describe a rare case of spinal toxoplasmosis presenting as myelitis in an adult with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in New Zealand.
PRESENTATION: A 38-year-old woman with SLE, lupus nephritis and myocarditis, treated with hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil and recently increased prednisone, presented with right-sided sciatica progressing to rapid bilateral leg weakness. Investigations included contrast MRI of the spine and brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and T12 laminectomy with repeat biopsy for histology and PCR.
RESULTS: MRI showed a ring-enhancing intramedullary T12 lesion with cord expansion and oedema to T8. CSF protein was elevated. Repeat biopsy revealed tachyzoites and PCR confirmed Toxoplasma gondii DNA, diagnosing necrotising toxoplasmosis myelitis. She received pyrimethamine, clindamycin and folinic acid with reduced immunosuppression. Follow-up MRI showed new basal ganglia lesions, prompting Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis, after which imaging stabilised. Six months later, her myocarditis progressed, and she died from cardiac arrest.
CONCLUSIONS: Toxoplasmosis should be considered in immunosuppressed patients with myelopathy and intramedullary lesions. Early diagnosis, prophylaxis consideration and reduction of immunosuppression where feasible are critical to preventing irreversible neurological deficits.
